item.title: Eloelo's Saurabh Pandey bets that Dolphin AI can break the gatekeepers of Indian storytelling
item.description: The Eloelo Group founder says AI-led production could turn India's storytellers into a global export force.
item.content:encoded:
When James Cameron's epic sci-fi movie Avatar hit cinemas in late 2000s, plenty of Indians watched it and wondered why we weren't making films like that. According to Saurabh Pandey, Founder and CEO of Eloelo Group, that question is about to lose its force.

Eloelo is an Indian live social entertainment and social gaming platform headquartered in Bengaluru. It was launched in 2020 by former Flipkart executives Pandey and Akshay Dubey. The platform bridges video/audio livestreaming with interactive gaming tailored specifically for India's youth and vernacular markets.

At the 17th edition of TechSparks, YourStory's flagship event, Pandey showed off Dolphin AI, Eloelo's AI video creation tool, in a session titled 'Can AI turn India into a global content export hub?', moderated by Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project.

Dolphin AI currently has a waitlist, with the platform releasing invite codes in batches.

For now, Dolphin AI is free as Eloelo is giving away generous early credits so creators can make their first few videos and get a feel for the solution. However, a credit-based pricing model will arrive eventually. Pandey said the team mainly wants to see how people use Dolphin AI, and early signs are promising: roughly 15,000 videos were built in about eight days, mostly through organic discovery.

The end of the budget bottleneck

Pandey's pitch centres on who gets to tell big stories. In the VFX era, he said, movie making belonged to whoever had the money. A good storyteller with a period drama in mind simply could not afford the visuals it demanded, and that made budgets the real gatekeeper of content.

AI is a total game-changer, he argued. Production usually eats up 50 to 60% of revenue in this category, squeezing distribution budgets and destroying unit economics. By slashing those production costs, creator imagination finally gets the breathing room it needs to thrive.

Distribution, meanwhile, has become largely algorithmic. A creator in India now competes for attention in the US or Europe on the same footing as anyone else.

Why this time might be different

The conversation then moved to another area of content that is seeing traction: micro-drama and short-form content. These have attracted plenty of Indian startups, yet few have become popular.

In India, he said, the top four or five micro-drama players together are running at more than Rs 5,000 crore, a level they reached in just 18 months.

He also pointed to South Korea, a country of 52 million people that has built a $15-billion content export economy. India has 1.4 billion people and no shortage of creative talent, he said. What it has lacked is intent, technology, ambition and capital. Too many Indian creators, in his view, still focus only on local audience. Nobody asks whether a new LLM is launching for India, he noted; it just launches for the world. Why shouldn't Indian stories do the same?

Platforms will consolidate, but supply is wide open

Pandey doesn't expect micro-drama to escape the pattern seen elsewhere. Food delivery, quick commerce, ecommerce and ride-hailing all ended up with two or three heavily funded players holding 70 to 75% of the market, and he expects the same for content.

The real opportunity, he said, lies on the supply side.

Eloelo launched about 200 new micro-dramas last month, roughly five or six a night, and works with around 90 production houses. His advice to would-be founders is to skip the platform race and build lean AI studios instead: a handful of writers, editors, promo producers and a line producer who could feed micro-dramas, OTT content and exportable IP to the big platforms.

He also had a message for writers and producers wary of AI. Use it as a brainstorming partner, he said, and ship more. As an example, he floated an idea close to his heart. An AI Ramayana already exists, but nobody has yet made a spectacular AI Mahabharata.

Eloelo has grown from one platform to five within the same group, Pandey said, and an IPO is not on the cards anytime soon. The focus is on growing profitably and sustainably.

item.title: Angel One, Zerodha expand US stock investing access for Indian investors
item.description: This reflects a broader push by Indian investment platforms to expand beyond domestic equities as retail investors seek exposure to global markets.
item.content:encoded:
Angel One and Zerodha are expanding access to the US stock markets for Indian investors, as domestic brokerages look to tap into the growing demand for international equities and portfolio diversification.

Angel One has begun rolling out US stock investing on its app, allowing users to invest in US-listed stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) alongside their Indian portfolios. The facility is currently available to a limited group of users, with a wider rollout expected by mid-November.

Investors will be able to buy shares of companies such as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Netflix, Spotify and Toyota. The platform will also support fractional investing, allowing users to purchase a portion of a share rather than an entire unit.

Meanwhile, Zerodha has also launched US stock investing in beta, offering access to around 2,000 US-listed stocks and 1,000 ETFs through its platform. The move gives Indian investors another avenue to access global businesses, particularly in sectors such as artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and semiconductors.

The expansion follows regulatory approval from the International Financial Services Centres Authority for brokers to offer international investing through GIFT City in Gujarat.

Angel One will waive brokerage charges until December 2026. From January 2027, it will charge 0.1% per trade, subject to a minimum brokerage of $0.99. Account opening, maintenance, deposits, and withdrawals will be free, although regulatory charges, GST, and foreign-exchange conversion costs will apply.

Zerodha's offering is being introduced in beta, with brokerage and other applicable charges governed by its published pricing structure.

Investments through these platforms are subject to the Reserve Bank of India's Liberalised Remittance Scheme and applicable regulatory requirements. Angel One has also said eligible US securities will carry Securities Investor Protection Corporation protection of up to $500,000, subject to applicable conditions.

The launches reflect a broader push by Indian investment platforms to expand beyond domestic equities as retail investors seek exposure to global markets. Platforms including Groww, Upstox and INDmoney also offer routes to international investing, intensifying competition in the segment.

item.title: How Operation Sindoor reshaped India's private defence tech industry
item.description: From faster procurement to direct engagement with the armed forces, Operation Sindoor has opened new opportunities for private defence companies developing critical military technologies.
item.content:encoded:
Following Operation Sindoor, India's private defence technology sector is seeing a shift in how the armed forces engage with domestic manufacturers. The transformation is marked by faster procurement, greater private-sector participation, and renewed emphasis on developing critical military technologies domestically, according to industry executives.

At TechSparks 2026, Ankit Kumar, Co-founder and Chief Business Officer of Tonbo Imaging; Priyanka Singhal, Founder and CEO of Ammunic Systems; and Radhika P, Co-founder of Pinaka Aerospace; discussed how Indian private companies contributed to recent military operations and what the country must prioritise to prepare for the battlefield of 2035.

In a panel discussion titled 'War Room 2035: What technologies must India build for the battlefield' moderated by Adith Charlie, Managing Editor of YourStory and The CapTable, the founders pointed to growing opportunities for indigenous companies in night-vision systems, electronic warfare, smart munitions, and autonomous defence platforms.

Operation Sindoor and the private sector's growing role

Priyanka Singhal, Founder and CEO of Ammunic Systems, a defence R&D firm specialising in electronic fuzes and munition technologies, described Operation Sindoor as a turning point for the industry. “The operation was an eye opener,” she said, adding that it had exposed the limitations of traditional defence procurement cycles.

Singhal said Ammunic supplied loitering munitions and gravity-drop bombs during Operation Sindoor, working with drone platform partners to integrate its weapons into systems used in the operation. According to her, the armed forces have begun moving away from an excessive focus on procedural compliance towards deploying equipment that meets immediate battlefield requirements. Initiatives such as iDEX and emergency procurement mechanisms have helped accelerate the process, she said.

Radhika P of Pinaka Aerospace echoed this assessment. Previously, private defence companies often worked through defence public sector undertakings (DPSUs), the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), and other established channels. Following Operation Sindoor, she said, the armed forces had increasingly engaged directly with private companies, particularly in electronic warfare, avionics, and sensor technologies.

Radhika said Pinaka had contributed to the indigenisation of missile systems that were deployed during the operation. She argued that the effectiveness of military equipment increasingly depends on its payloads, including sensors and electronic warfare systems, rather than the platform alone.

“If there is an electronic countermeasure system, it can neutralise a platform which is probably 10 times more expensive,” she said, underscoring the strategic importance of developing indigenous payload technologies.

Kumar of Tonbo Imaging, which specialises in electro-optical and infrared technologies, said the shift towards indigenous defence procurement had begun even before Operation Sindoor, particularly following developments along India's eastern border. That had encouraged the armed forces to reduce their dependence on technologies sourced from countries sharing land borders with India.

Tonbo, which has spent nearly two decades developing indigenous imaging systems, was positioned to benefit from that shift, Kumar said. Its night-vision technologies have been deployed across several Indian military operations, including Operation Sindoor, when air-defence systems used the company's capabilities, he added.

Kumar said close engagement with the armed forces, including product trials and feedback from users, had helped Tonbo develop its technologies. “We've learned things the hard way. We've learned things on the ground. We've learned things with the customers,” he said.

What India must build by 2035

Looking towards 2035, Kumar said defence systems would increasingly move towards autonomy, reducing the need for direct human involvement in certain operations. He pointed to the potential use of autonomous systems in air combat and on the ground, including the possibility of humanoid robots supporting border operations.

As military platforms become more autonomous, sensors and intelligence will become critical to their ability to detect threats, interpret their surroundings and respond without constant human intervention.

“For autonomy, sensors, intelligence, both are very critical, very important,” Kumar said. 

He argued that India had strengths in both areas, particularly in developing intelligence capabilities that can operate directly on military platforms. Such technologies, he said, could improve operational efficiency and reduce dependence on human operators, but they needed to be developed as sovereign capabilities rather than sourced from overseas suppliers.

“Intelligence, connectivity, sensing, these will be the mainstay of how the wars will be fought tomorrow,” he said.

For Radhika, a key battlefield priority is control over the electromagnetic spectrum, which underpins radar, communications, electronic warfare, and several other military capabilities. She argued that future military advantage would increasingly depend on how effectively forces detect, interpret and disrupt electromagnetic signals.

That also makes ownership of the underlying technology critical. Developing or assembling defence platforms in India is not sufficient if the software, electronics architecture and intellectual property remain controlled by foreign suppliers.

“It is very important to have good control on the source code, the board design, and things like that,” Radhika said.

She also emphasised that technology transfer should strengthen India's ability to develop and integrate systems independently, rather than create continued dependence on overseas suppliers. Control over intellectual property and systems integration would be especially important in reducing the risks associated with foreign supply chains, she added.

Closing the gaps in research and deployment

Singhal, meanwhile, called for greater integration across the three armed services.

She argued that the Army, Navy and Air Force needed better-connected platforms and weapons systems to coordinate effectively during emergencies. She also highlighted materials research as an area requiring greater attention.

Advanced materials would play an increasingly important role in developing next-generation weapon systems, including those requiring greater effectiveness and stealth capabilities. India, she said, needed to place more emphasis on materials R&D alongside investments in autonomous systems and other defence technologies.

The founders also identified persistent challenges in bringing together the armed forces, government research institutions and private industry. Singhal said startups and smaller defence companies could move faster than government research programmes, which often face bureaucratic delays.

Radhika said the challenge stemmed partly from differing expectations. The armed forces want sophisticated systems delivered quickly, research organisations operate through lengthy validation cycles and private manufacturers need commercially viable development timelines.

One way forward, she suggested, was to involve private industry from the prototype stage, with the armed forces funding development projects, research organisations working alongside manufacturers and clearer pathways to production orders.

She pointed to the Development-cum-Production Partner model as a mechanism that could help bridge the gap between research, development and large-scale manufacturing if implemented effectively.

For India's private defence technology industry, the next challenge is not simply to manufacture more equipment domestically. It is to develop and control the technologies that make military platforms effective, while building a procurement and research ecosystem capable of moving those technologies from the laboratory to the battlefield.

item.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 19, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Monday, October 19, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
From India’s artificial intelligence (AI) opportunity to how a Bengaluru hospital is paying doctors for recovery, not procedures, here are the latest developments across sectors.

Featured Stories

India's next tech edge according to CTOs

India’s technology industry has long relied on talent, cost efficiency and scale. But as artificial intelligence makes advanced tools more accessible, these advantages alone may no longer be enough to differentiate companies.

The next edge, according to technology leaders at TechSparks 2026, will come from how effectively companies use AI to solve specific problems, understand customers and build products that are difficult to replicate.

Read more

Funding News

Even Healthcare raises $50M in Series B round

Bengaluru-based managed care company Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a Series B round led by existing investor Khosla Ventures. Alpha Wave also participated in the round.

According to the company, the round values it at three times its valuation 18 months ago and brings its total funding to more than $120 million.

The money will go towards five new Even hospitals in Bengaluru over the next six months, beginning with Indiranagar. The company runs two hospitals in the city at present.

Read more

The Pant Project bags Rs 109 Cr to accelerate retail expansion

The Pant Project, a premium menswear label specialising in trousers and other bottomwear, has raised Rs 109 crore in a Series B funding round led by Mirae Asset Venture Investments.

Existing investor Sorin Investments also participated, alongside family offices and angel investors including Anisha Saraf, B&K Securities, MGA Ventures and B2V Ventures. The company has also secured venture debt from Alteria Capital, with IndigoEdge advising on the equity transaction.

Founded by brothers Dhruv and Udit Toshniwal, The Pant Project began as a digital-first business focused on fit, fabric performance and comfort for Indian men. Its products include Malai Pants and Inklock No Fade Black Jeans, and it sells through its website, Myntra, Amazon and physical stores.

Read more

Other News

AngelBot AI launches TeamSync to secure enterprise knowledge with AI-powered search

AngelBot AI has launched TeamSync, an AI-native platform designed to help enterprises securely search, manage and extract insights from fragmented documents and information repositories.

The platform combines natural-language document interaction, semantic search and permissions-aware AI, with citations and audit trails to support reliable information access. Its capabilities also include metadata extraction, electronic signatures, contract lifecycle management and eDiscovery.

Targeting mid-sized and large enterprises across regulated and document-intensive sectors, TeamSync offers subscription-based software, platform licensing and implementation services. The launch builds on AngelBot AI’s document management work, including IMIR, which has received recognition from the Indian Air Force.

VETO launches sports carnival, offers 300+ hours of subscription-free live sports

VETO, India’s subscription-free OTT platform, has launched the VETO Sports Carnival, offering more than 300 hours of live sports streaming across cricket, football, weightlifting and tennis during October and November.

The line-up includes an international ODI tri-series, Test matches, the IWF World Senior Championships, SAFF Championship, Billie Jean King Cup Play-offs and Davis Cup Finals.

The initiative expands VETO’s live sports portfolio as it seeks to make international sporting events accessible to Indian audiences without a subscription fee. The platform also offers 60+ live TV channels across 12 languages and more than 10 content genres.

Yes Madam revenue hits Rs 402 Cr annualised run rate, grows 3.9x in two years

At-home beauty and wellness platform Yes Madam has reported a 3.9-fold increase in revenue and 3.5-fold growth in Net Transaction Value (NTV) between Q2 FY25 and Q2 FY27. The company’s annualised revenue run rate reached Rs 402 crore, while its NTV run rate stood at Rs 836 crore.

In Q2 FY27, revenue rose 69% year-on-year to Rs 79.4 crore, while NTV grew 75% to Rs 165.8 crore.

Founded in 2016, Yes Madam operates across more than 55 cities with a network of 10,000-plus service professionals. The company plans to expand services, strengthen its network and invest in technology.

So/Facet raises Rs 10 Cr seed funding led by Sauce to build lab-grown diamond jewellery brand

So/Facet, a premium lab-grown diamond jewellery brand founded by former Unilever executives Aarushi Agrawal Naulakha and Abhishek Naulakha, has raised Rs10 crore in a seed funding round led by Sauce.

The company will use the capital for brand building, design, technology, hiring and an omnichannel retail expansion. Set to launch online in November 2026, So/Facet plans to open more than 30 premium stores over three years.

The brand aims to position lab-grown diamonds as expressions of personal style rather than jewellery reserved for traditional milestones. Its six launch collections feature IGI-certified diamonds and contemporary, in-house designs.

Guttify targets Tier II markets in three states, eyes 5x growth in annual recurring revenue

Gut-health startup Guttify plans to expand into select Tier II markets across Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Punjab through pilot initiatives in FY27, targeting fivefold growth in annual recurring revenue (ARR).

The company has served over 30,000 consumers and reported 67% quarter-on-quarter growth. Its Rs 399 DIY Gut Scan Kit sold approximately 15,000 units between January and August 2026, with around half of buyers subsequently purchasing other products.

Guttify plans to expand its portfolio with products including Poopie, a fibre-based constipation-support product, and RISE, a morning greens blend, while strengthening personalised recommendations, consumer education and expert guidance.

As You Asked raises Rs 45 lakh pre-seed funding to expand children’s nutrition products

As You Asked, a nutrition startup focused on children aged 2–12, has raised Rs 45 lakh in an equity-funded pre-seed round backed by ISB D-Labs and angel investors. The company will use the funds to support its market launch, product development, manufacturing and distribution.

Its planned portfolio includes daily nutrition powders, hydration mixes and micronutrient gummies without added sugars. The startup has engaged more than 100 parents, conducted over 200 child taste tests and run an early pilot involving 200-plus customers to inform its product development. It aims to make everyday nutrition simpler, accessible and easier for families to incorporate into daily routines.

item.title: Data, not chips, will decide India’s AI and biotech future, say deeptech founders
item.description: Founders from CoreMantle and Loopworm say India must own context-rich data to scale AI and biotech and cut reliance on imports.
item.content:encoded:
When people talk about technology infrastructure, they usually mean semiconductors, data centres, and AI models. But the layer that decides how well these technologies work is the data underneath them, and India still has to build it.

At a panel discussion on 'The invisible infrastructure of the new tech order' at TechSparks 2026, moderated by Chhavi Mahajan, Chief Content Officer, YourStory, the panellists said India’s advantage will come from owning trusted, context-rich data in fields ranging from language AI to biotech.

Arvind Pani, Founder, CoreMantle, an AI data intelligence startup, said data is the one part of the technology stack that cannot be swapped out. “You can continue to replace compute. You can continue to replace the application, but you cannot replace the data,” he said.

Ankit Bagaria, Co-founder and CEO, Loopworm, an insect biotechnology company, said the gap is especially wide in biopharma, where too much work still happens through trial and error. Better data, he said, could cut the time it takes to bring a product to market.

Bagaria said biotech deserves the same attention as AI, quantum and chips, particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic. He noted that India still imports about 73% of its key materials, including active pharmaceutical ingredients and reagents, from China. And although the country supplies a large share of the world’s vaccines by volume, that accounts for only about 5% of the market by value.

“We have operated in the biosimilar space for a very, very long time, where somebody else is discovering the molecules for us,” he said. He argued that India now needs to move into drug discovery.

Pani said the same need for local context applies to language. India’s internet was built for English users, which put up two barriers at once for most citizens, who had to learn the technology and a new language. Only about 4 to 5% of India’s population is comfortable using English alone, he noted.

He added that even English is not a solved problem for AI. Models trained mostly on American English often struggle with Australian or regional accents, and English as spoken across Indian states varies widely. “These are the nuances that nobody else will understand, that India will understand,” he said.

Both panellists agreed that a bigger dataset is not necessarily a better one. Pani said AI models built on smaller amounts of enriched, contextual data outperform those trained on large volumes of raw data. Many Indian language datasets are recorded in studios from scripts, he noted, so models trained on them perform well in controlled settings but fail in real-world conversations.

Bagaria said that across biological data, “it’s garbage in, garbage out.”

Loopworm spent about 12 to 13 months cleaning existing data while building a digital tool that maps the inner workings of the silkworm. The work had to be tailored to Indian silkworm strains and the pathogens that affect them.

Loopworm uses silkworms to produce sustainable animal feed and high-value recombinant proteins.

Bagaria said Loopworm chose silkworm because silk is over 98% protein, which makes the insect one of nature’s most efficient converters of plant leaves into protein. The silkworm has been domesticated for about 4,000 years, its genome was sequenced in 2007, and around 175 institutes in India teach sericulture and related biotech.

He added that this data-led approach has already cut a set of experiments from 10 months and Rs 25 lakh to two and a half months and about Rs 4.5 lakh. “I am sure that in 10 years’ time, all of us would be saying that the largest impact of AI has come on biotech,” he said.

Pani said proprietary data is already becoming a competitive moat. He cited legal AI company Harvey, which has changed both its models and its compute while keeping its domain-specific data as its core advantage.

On what needs to change, Pani said India must design technology for its own needs. He recalled that his previous company brought Indian language support to Android in 2011 through a partnership with Qualcomm, before Google did. “If we continue to think that somebody else is going to solve our problem, then we will always be behind the curve,” he said.

Bagaria welcomed government initiatives such as the BioE3 policy and the Research, Development and Innovation Fund. But he called for more public and foundational funding for basic data generation, such as the in-depth sequencing and characterisation of Indian organisms, because traditional investors are unlikely to fund fundamental science.

item.title: Hunar.AI raises Rs 40 Cr in Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures
item.description: Hunar.AI is focused on developing specialised AI technology for frontline-intensive industries. The company will use the funds for building AI infrastructure, product development, and go-to-market expansion.
item.content:encoded:
Hunar.AI has raised Rs 40 crore in a Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures. The round also saw participation from Hyderabad Angels Fund, Together Fund, Seedstars, AVNM Ventures, PhysicsWallah co-founders Prateek Maheshwari and Alakh Pandey, and MediaMint co-founder Aditya Vuchi.

Hunar.AI will use the funds for building AI infrastructure, product development, and go-to-market expansion. The company is focused on developing specialised AI technology for frontline-intensive industries, where high-volume hiring, geographically distributed teams, and language diversity create operational challenges that conventional HR systems struggle to address.

“Frontline workforce management is one of the largest yet most underserved opportunities in enterprise AI. Solving it requires more than applying general-purpose models to existing processes. It demands a deep understanding of industry workflows, multilingual capabilities and technology that can reliably execute tasks at scale,” said Krishna Khandelwal, Co-founder and CEO, Hunar.AI.

Founded in 2022 by Krishna Khandelwal and Shantanu Bhattacharyya, Hunar’s platform comprises Hunar Voice and Hunar Connect, which use conversational AI agents to manage workforce workflows through voice, WhatsApp and chat. Workflows include candidate sourcing and screening, interview scheduling, onboarding, training, employee engagement and worker retention. By automating high-volume interactions, the platform helps enterprises manage frontline workforce processes while maintaining communication with candidates and employees across locations.

Arpit Agrawal, Partner at Blume Ventures said, “As the world looks to India for lessons in managing these new-age businesses at scale, Hunar is building the AI layer that makes them possible. By focusing on outcomes rather than infrastructure, Hunar has the potential to build a category in India that can scale globally.”

According to a statement, Hunar’s AI agents handled over 15 million conversations in September 2026, with conversation volumes doubling every quarter. Its clients include Swiggy, Delhivery, Instamart, Pronto, Blue Dart, Flipkart, Aditya Birla Capital and Tata Croma.

NITI Aayog projects that India’s gig workforce will grow from around 1 crore workers in 2024–25 to 2.35 crore by 2029–30. As enterprises expand across cities and regions, hiring, onboarding and retaining workers efficiently has become an important operational priority, with many processes still dependent on manual calls, repeated follow-ups and coordination.
